content: Antiretroviral therapy (ARV) drugs are medications specifically designed to treat HIV infection. The use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) involves a combination of three or more ARV drugs to manage HIV effectively. ART is a lifelong treatment and is also referred to as combination ART or highly active ART (HAART). ARV drugs are also utilized for HIV prevention. This includes preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding, reducing HIV transmission to serodiscordant sexual partners, and preventing HIV acquisition in individuals exposed to the virus through post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Viral suppression is achieved when the viral load in a patient’s blood is reduced to levels below the detection threshold of standard viral assays. Conversely, viral failure occurs when viral suppression cannot be achieved or maintained, defined as a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL after at least six months of ART, despite adherence support. Universal access to ART is defined as achieving high treatment coverage (80% or more of the eligible population) that is both accessible and affordable. However, this does not necessarily imply 100% coverage. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV involves the use of ARV drugs to prevent HIV transmission from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, delivery, and breastfeeding. Previous WHO guidelines have categorized PMTCT strategies into “Options A, B, and B+.” Combination HIV prevention integrates behavioral, biomedical, and structural approaches to maximize the impact on reducing HIV transmission and acquisition. Early infant diagnosis involves testing infants for HIV following potential exposure during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. Point-of-care testing is conducted at or near the site of care delivery, providing rapid results to facilitate timely clinical decision-making. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and/or HIV p24 antigen using immunochromatographic or immunofiltration methods. PEP refers to the use of ARV drugs by individuals not infected with HIV but potentially exposed to the virus to prevent infection. PrEP involves the use of ARV drugs by HIV-negative individuals to prevent HIV acquisition. Lay providers are individuals trained to deliver specific healthcare services without formal professional or paraprofessional certification. Midwives are healthcare workers who have completed a recognized midwifery education program, including registered midwives, community midwives, and nurse-midwives. Non-physician clinicians are professional healthcare workers capable of performing many diagnostic and clinical functions of a physician but are not formally trained as physicians. These include health officers, clinical officers, physician assistants, nurse practitioners, and nurse clinicians, who play a critical role in HIV care and treatment in some countries. Nurses are individuals authorized to practice nursing or trained in basic nursing skills. This category includes registered nurses, clinical nurse specialists, licensed nurses, auxiliary nurses, dental nurses, and primary care nurses. Task shifting and task sharing involve redistributing tasks between healthcare workers with longer training and those with shorter training, such as lay providers, to optimize service delivery. Adherence refers to the extent to which a person’s behavior—such as taking medication, following a diet, or making lifestyle changes—aligns with agreed recommendations from a healthcare provider. The continuum of HIV care encompasses a comprehensive package of HIV testing, prevention, treatment, and care services for individuals at risk of acquiring HIV, people living with HIV, and their families. Examples of services within the continuum of care include combination HIV prevention (e.g., PrEP), HIV testing and linkage to care, management of opportunistic infections and comorbid conditions, initiation and monitoring of ART, switching to secondor third-line ART, and palliative care. Dispensing ART involves providing medication to individuals already on ART between regular clinic visits, assessing new symptoms, and offering adherence monitoring and support. Distribution of ART refers to the physical transportation of ARV drugs, which can be categorized into wholesale distribution (large quantities over long distances), clinic distribution or refill (specific drugs for known users), and community distribution (limited quantities over short distances for specific individuals). Integrated health services ensure a continuum of health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care across different levels and sites of care within the health system, tailored to individual needs throughout their lives. Linkage refers to the process of supporting individuals testing for HIV or diagnosed with HIV to engage with prevention, treatment, and care services appropriate to their status. For people with HIV, this begins with diagnosis and ends with enrollment in care or treatment. Retention in HIV care means that a person living with HIV, enrolled in care, routinely attends services as needed. This excludes individuals who have died or are lost to follow-up. People-centered health services adopt a care approach that prioritizes the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, viewing them as participants and beneficiaries of trusted health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. People-centered care requires education and support to enable individuals to make decisions and participate in their care, focusing on health needs and expectations rather than diseases. A public health approach addresses the collective health needs of a population rather than focusing solely on individual cases. This approach aims to ensure broad access to high-quality services and medicines at the population level, using simplified and standardized methods, while balancing the best-proven standards of care with feasibility in resource-limited settings.
